Reviewer 1:
This work by She et al. provides a comprehensive longitudinal examination of S. aureus (SA) colonization and
infection among patients in the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia NICU. Progress in infection control and
mitigation has stalled over the past 10 years pointing to severe knowledge gaps in our understanding of
carriage and transmission. This work provides a significant contribution to that end. The rationale for the study
is sound, the methods are solid, and the results and conclusion are mostly appropriate.
Methodological strengths of this work include a large number of children sampled over multiple time points,
collection from asymptomatic carriage as well as infections, focus on all SA (not just MRSA), extensive patient
metadata data, and use of whole genome sequencing (WGS) for high-resolution assessment of evolutionary
links. Such large-scale sampling that includes longitudinal samples and WGS is extremely rare!
The attempt to tie strain types to transmission, invasive disease, and persistence is noteworthy with extremely
valuable potential to translate surveillance efforts into mitigation, and disease prevention. While there have
been a small number of studies that explored genetic features associated with the transition from colonization to
invasion, pathogenicity, and infection persistence
(https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.165415.113, https://doi.org/10.1128/msystems.00378-
22, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.77195, https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.01000-
07, https://doi.org/10.1016/J.CHOM.2023.03.009), I am not aware of studies that link strains (or their
components) to asymptomatic persistence and transmission. This is an important line of current research efforts
to which this work will make a valuable contribution.
Author response: We thank the Reviewer for the comments. We have added specific responses to each
comment below.
Specific comments:
1. I appreciate the authors pointing out that transmission could be mediated by contaminated
environments/equipment, and caregivers, but what other mechanisms of transmission seem possible?
Could direct transmission be occurring or transition from a parent to infants that are not theirs?
Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for this important observation. We agree that multiple transmission mechanisms
are possible. Parent-to-infant transmission, including cross-transmission where parents may transfer S.
aureus between their own baby and others, represents another potential route that cannot be excluded
based on our current analysis. We acknowledge this as a limitation of our study, as we did not collect
samples from parents or other family members who may serve as reservoirs for transmission.
Additionally, direct transmission is theoretically possible, but it would likely still be mediated by
healthcare workers, as infants in the NICU have limited mobility and remain primarily in their
individual bed spaces. Finally, contamination of the patients’ immediate environment, shared spaces for
caregivers of patients, and shared equipment that is moved around the NICU from patient to patient
could be additional sources of transmission. We have expanded our Discussion section (lines 308-313)
to explicitly address alternative transmission routes.
2. In my opinion, author’s use of spatial data to further parse the effects of distance on transmission is not
warranted or needed. While the distance of spread within each NICU section may provide some
biological insight into mechanisms of spread, it is hard for me to imagine why distances between NICU
sections are considered when an infant may be transported just as easily between distant and adjacent
sections. As such, while the presence of a colonized/infected individual within a section increases risk to
others in the same section, the impact of larger distances (between sections) on transmission is likely
completely anthropogenic. I suggest that the authors remove these additional analyses (including the
rescaled phylogeny) as they complicated this work and don’t seem to be needed to support the
conclusions – Alternatively, provide better justification for their inclusion.
Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for this insightful critique regarding the spatial distance analysis. Following the
Reviewer's recommendation, we have relocated the spatial distance rescaled phylogeny analysis to the
Extended Data Figure S8,9 with a brief mention in the Discussion (lines 291-295). We now frame this
analysis as an exploratory approach that may have utility for understanding transmission dynamics but
requires further studies to validate the epidemiological significance. We have streamlined the main text
to focus on our core findings, particularly the correlation between patient numbers and persistence as a
measure of transmissibility, which remains robust independent of the spatial analysis.
3. Perhaps the most important weakness of this work is that there is limited discussion of an alternative
(null) hypothesis: By chance alone (not due to any intrinsic genetic characteristic or adaptive
evolution), some clones will have better fitness (at some point they were able to proliferate – perhaps
shed in higher numbers by a single source, or were in an infant that was placed near others – in other
words, they were in the right place at the right time). A high-fitness clone would be expected to be more
likely to colonize additional persons, be shed into the environment, and persist for longer periods of time
- even in the absence of any adaptive differences between strains. Importantly, such clones would also
be more likely to cause invasive disease simply by persisting in an environment with many
immunosuppressed individuals subject to invasive procedures. As such, while transmission seems to
predict invasive disease (as stated in the title), this may not be due to the presence of certain strains or
genes, but rather because SA is widely circulating. Authors need to better modulate the discussion of
their results in light of this – the single sentence in line 270 is not sufficient. If indeed this null
hypothesis is correct, then simply monitoring the load of SA around the NICU may be easier and more
useful than monitoring for specific strains or genes. These two scenarios are not mutually exclusive.
Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for this excellent and fundamental observation, which identifies a critical
alternative hypothesis that the observed correlation between transmission and invasive infections may
result from stochastic events rather than intrinsic genetic characteristics. Our current data cannot
distinguish between the two hypotheses, and the hypotheses, as Reviewer suggests, likely operate
simultaneously and are not mutually exclusive. Future studies are needed to investigate the contributions
of those factors to transmission dynamics in the NICU settings. We have substantially expanded our
Discussion (lines 327-333) to address this alternative hypothesis.
4. About SNP thresholds: I see these as being a guide for identifying transmission events or even intra-host
diversity. It is unfortunate that the term “threshold” is commonly used as it suggests a hard cut-off
rather than a guide. It is widely recognized that the resolution in any clade is maximized when SNP
discovery and phylogenetic analysis is restricted to members of that clade, and thus a hierarchical
approach to zoom in on a given clade is widely practiced. However, the application of this concept has
been slow in guiding transmission determination. While this method is not novel, I have never seen such
a thorough demonstration of this concept – and this will be of value to a broad set of readers. In short,
the authors show that the concept of a “threshold” is not valid. I would thus encourage the authors to
use their analyses as a justification for moving beyond the “threshold” concept. Can the authors think
of a more appropriate descriptor than a “threshold approach”? I think that authors can state that the
number of SNPs found within a clone varied between x and y and this was in line with previous work,
instead of applying a “threshold”. Also, your hierarchical snp threshold approach may be better
described as being “clade-specific” rather than “corrected for phylogenetic structure” (Line 113).
Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for recognizing the value of our approach and for this insightful critique of the
"threshold" terminology. We agree that "threshold" might inappropriately imply a hard cutoff rather than
the dynamic, clade-specific approach we employ. We would also like to point out that our approach is
both “clade-specific” and “phylogeny corrected”. That is, we first limit our threshold-finding algorithm
to each subclade of the broad phylogeny. Then, once a strain has been determined (in this case by
finding a “plateau” where no new genomes are added to a group as the threshold is increased) we then
map these genomes back to the phylogenetic tree to ensure that groups are monophyletic and have
strong bootstrap support. In our revised manuscript, we have rewritten this section to clarify this point,
and we have introduced the term “phylothreshold” to summarize this approach. We have automated this
approach in the “Thresher” pipeline that is available on GitHub
(github.com/microbialARC/THRESHER).
We quantified within-cluster SNP distances across all 69 transmission clusters. A mean distance of 23.9
SNPs (SD,12.60; median 22 [Q1-Q3, 15-30]) was found. Individual cluster distributions are shown in
Figure R1d. We then compared our results to 40 published S. aureus transmission studies to validate our
approach. We have incorporated Extended Data Table S3 with details of all 40 studies. The results
demonstrated that the phylothresholds determined using our approach align well with those reported in
the literature when grouped by clonal complex (Figure R1a). Studies without hard cutoffs also showed
SNP distributions consistent with ours (Figure R1b,c).
We note that some studies report narrower SNP ranges due to shorter study periods. For example,
Gideskog et al. found 0-7 SNPs over one month (Study ID 34) and Eyre et al. found 0-3 SNPs over three
months (Study ID 39). Additionally, methodological differences in SNP calling tools and reference
genomes can affect absolute SNP values.
This comparative analysis provides preliminary validation that our clade-specific approach captures
genetic relatedness that is consistent with established transmission studies. In our revised manuscript, we
have added Extended Data Figure S2(Figure R1) to visualize this comparative validation. We are
currently working on systematic validation through simulated outbreak and reanalysis of publicly
available datasets using our approach to further confirm the accuracy.

Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for highlighting this. We have revised this text at lines 484-485 to improve
clarity, and we provide our rationale for using publicly available genomes below.
The Thresher pipeline tests SNP thresholds from the minimum SNP distance up to 500 SNPs within
each clade determined by hierarchical clustering, using a plateau method to determine optimal strain
compositions. However, if the plateau is reached at excessively high values, the resulting clusters may
include genetically distant genomes that represent broader epidemiological connections rather than
transmission events within our NICU setting.
Our approach uses publicly available S. aureus genomes as checkpoints to validate the SNP thresholds
used for defining the compositions of transmission clusters. We assume that publicly available S. aureus
genomes should not be part of NICU transmission clusters. When strain compositions begin
incorporating public genomes, this indicates the SNP threshold has become too high and is capturing
genetic relatedness beyond our study scope. We used a 1000 SNP threshold to exclude genomes from
downstream fine-grained analysis, which create long phylogenetic branches in the clade-specific
phylogeny and could compromise accuracy of the analysis. The excluded genomes are considered
singletons. This 1000-SNP threshold was informed by our SNP distance matrix analysis (Figure R2),
which showed that distances of >1000 SNPs typically represent comparisons between genomes that
belong to different sequence types, making the compared genomes highly unlikely within the same
transmission cluster.

To address this concern, we performed two analyses to assess sampling bias. First, using TransPhylo

false negative rates

transmission clusters (Figure 2) is based on the assumption that genomic emergence is equivalent to
epidemiological emergence - however, phylogenetic trees are not transmission trees
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28100788/). For example, the authors have mapped dates of the most
recent common ancestor (tMRCA) for transmission clusters against admission dates for putative index
cases for each cluster. However, the date a bacterial strain "emerges" through genetic evolution is
independent of the movement of the bacterium's host (the patient). Furthermore, the first patient
detected with S aureus colonisation is not necessarily the source of transmission in an outbreak. Given
the timespan, how would transmission within the NICU be distinguished from vertical transmission (e.g.
two neonates acquiring S aureus from the same mother, or transmission between mothers rather than
between neonates)?
Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for this important methodological point. We acknowledge that genomic
emergence does not necessarily correspond to epidemiological emergence or transmission index case.
We implemented TransPhylo analysis to address these concerns. The results revealed that the medoid
transmission index dates fell within the 95% highest posterior density intervals of tMRCA, with 95%
confidence intervals of transmission index dates overlapping with the 95% HPD of tMRCA for all 48
clusters. This concordance suggests that tMRCA serves as both an indicator of genomic emergence and
a reliable proxy for transmission index cases at least in our dataset.
We have updated Figure 2b with TransPhylo results, added detailed TransPhylo methodology in the
Methods section, revised the Results section to incorporate transmission tree analysis, and made all
analysis scripts publicly available in our GitHub repository. These analyses strengthen our interpretation
while acknowledging the complexity of distinguishing healthcare-associated transmission from other
potential routes, including vertical transmission between mothers and neonates.
9. The underlying message that patients who are closer in proximity and in time are more likely to have the
same strain is not a particularly novel message. I think the more interesting messages lie in the
exceptions to the rule - why were some isolates from different patients separated in time and space (e.g.
by 3 years in different sections) part of the same clone? Were these patients related to others in the
cluster or were there opportunities for transmission outside the NICU?
Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that the exceptions to the rule are worth
deeper analysis and have expanded our discussion of these findings in the results section (lines 186-
192).
Our analysis revealed that 60.9% (42/69) of transmission clusters demonstrated strong epidemiological
links through both spatial proximity and overlapping treatment team assignments. About 27.5% (19/69:
Clusters 16, 29, 32, 33, 35, 37, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 46, 47, 49, 54, 62, 64, and 66) of clusters showed
links only through shared NICU sections, while one cluster (1.4%: Cluster 55) had overlapping
treatment teams without shared NICU section observed.
Notably, 10.1% of clusters (7/69: Clusters 34, 38, 49, 57, 58, 59, and 63) exhibited no epidemiological
links in our analysis (Extended Data Figures S3-S5). The SNP distances within these clusters confirmed
accurate strain determination by our pipeline, suggesting that analytical artifacts are unlikely (Extended
Data Figure S2d).
As the Reviewer suggested, these exceptions likely reflect transmission routes not captured in our study.
Potential explanations include transmission through unsampled intermediary patients, contaminated
shared equipment, environmental reservoirs, or vertical transmission from parents—mechanisms that
would not be apparent from spatial proximity or treatment team assignments alone.

11. More information on the infection prevention and control measures used within the NICUs during the
study would assist readers for context and interpretation. Were there any changes in policy during the
study? For patients identified with MSSA/MRSA colonisation, what measures were undertaken? In the
discussion, lines 272-274 suggest that infection prevention and control measures could reduce the risk
of invasive infection - this should be the risk of transmission. The only measure that has been shown to
reduce the risk of invasive infection is decolonisation (in adults colonised with S aureus), though to my
knowledge this has not been demonstrated in neonates. Note there are also risks associated with
chlorhexidine administration in neonates.
Author response:
During the timeframe of the study, the NICU and Infection Prevention and Control teams were actively
engaged in quality improvement and infection prevention efforts to decrease S. aureus colonization and
infection rates, in addition to ongoing efforts to prevent healthcare associated infections. All infants
identified to be positive with either MSSA or MRSA based on surveillance or results of diagnostic
testing for clinical indication, underwent decolonization with a 5-day course of mupirocin, starting in
July 2022. All infants with central venous catheters (term corrected age or older) received daily
chlorhexidine bathing. The NICU also embarked on a hand hygiene and ‘bare below the elbows’
campaign in July 2022 to re-engage staff in infection prevention efforts. Finally, the NICU added
initiatives to enhance cleaning procedures for NICU patient rooms through the course of the study.
12. From an implementation in clinical practice perspective, what was the median time from colonisation to
invasive infection and from colonisation to onwards transmission? Would it have been feasible to
identify colonisation, sequence the isolate and implement decolonisation measures to reduce the risk of
invasive infection, or control measures to reduce the risk of onwards transmission? If not feasible, some
of the discussion could be reframed around more realistic implementations of the approach - for
example, triggering infection control interventions such as point prevalence surveys across the unit,
universal decolonisation, enhanced unit cleaning and staff re-education around hand hygiene to
interrupt persistence of particular strains associated with a high incidence of invasive disease.
Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for this important clinical perspective on implementation feasibility. We
analyzed the temporal patterns and present the following findings:
(1) We captured the progression of 19 patients (19/618) from colonization to invasive infection with the
same strain. The median interval was 19 days (Q1-Q3, 9-138, mean, 66.95).
(2) At the strain level, for the 19 strains associated with both colonization and invasive infection (10 of
which were transmission clusters), the median interval from earliest colonization to earliest invasive
infection was 147 days (Q1-Q3, 14-245, mean, 156.47).
(3) Among the 69 transmission clusters identified, the median length from earliest detection to earliest
transmission event was 91 days (Q1-Q3, 18-210, mean: 131.10).
We acknowledge that the variable intervals likely reflect multiple confounding factors, including strain-
specific genetic traits and individual patient susceptibility, which requires further investigation for better
interpret these results. However, these results suggest that there is likely an adequate interval of time
available in many cases, once the colonizing strain is identified, to feasibly implement measures to
decolonize patients, reduce environmental bioburden, or both. We hypothesize that implementation of
this targeted approach for strains known to be at high risk of transmission and invasive infection, above
and beyond general infection control measures, may improve the effectiveness of efforts to decrease
transmission and invasive infections.

to the local NICU dataset than the Philadelphia dataset.
Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for seeking clarification on our methodology. The global database comprised
68,299 publicly available genomes from NCBI GenBank (as of April 2024), which contained limited
genomes from the Philadelphia area. Notably, the genomes with close genetic relatedness (≤100 SNP
distance) to our NICU isolates were collected from the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania,
located adjacent to our NICU.
The local Philadelphia database consisted of unpublished genomes not available in NCBI, serving as an
important comparator to demonstrate that the transmission events observed in our NICU were not
circulating more broadly in the local Philadelphia area. This comparison strengthens our evidence for
cryptic transmission events confined to the NICU setting, as these closely related strains were not
detected even outside our NICU in the community.
The inclusion of both global and local databases provides comprehensive context for interpreting the
genomic relatedness and transmission dynamics within our study.

17. Line 125: What were the non-NICU strains/clones in this study referred to in this paragraph? The study
methods only refer to collection of patient or environmental isolates of S aureus from the NICU.
Author response:
We thank the Reviewer for this comment. We have expanded the description of non-NICU isolates in
the Methods (lines 354-357) and Results (lines 137-142) and provided rationale for including non-NICU
isolates in the Methods (lines 355-357) and Discussion (lines 271-273) sections of our revised
manuscript, as detailed below.
While surveillance samples were restricted to NICU patients, S. aureus-positive blood culture isolates
collected hospital-wide as part of concurrent surveillance efforts at CHOP were included in our analysis.
These genomes served as "very local" controls to detect potential transmission events between the NICU
and other hospital locations. Additionally, including non-NICU isolates enabled continuous monitoring
of patients initially admitted to the NICU who subsequently transferred to other units, allowing us to
track potential NICU-acquired strains beyond NICU.
A total of 355 isolates from S. aureus-positive blood cultures were collected from 140 patients outside
the NICU. Of these 140 patients, 109 had no prior NICU admission, while 31 had been previously
admitted to the NICU. Among these 31 patients, only 12 had high-quality NICU genomes available for
analysis prior to transfer outside NICU.
From a clonality perspective, the 355 non-NICU genomes comprised 134 non-cluster strains: 57
singletons (57 genomes) and 77 clones (279 genomes). Notably, only 19 genomes belonged to 7
transmission clusters (Clusters 1, 2, 10, 29, 37, 51, and 58). None of the 57 singletons were observed in
the NICU. Of the 77 clones from 76 patients, only 4 clones were epidemiologically linked to the NICU.
Specifically, these 4 clones were isolated from 4 patients who had NICU admissions with positive
samples collected during their NICU stay, prior to transfer to other hospital units where subsequent non-
NICU isolates were obtained.
All 19 genomes involved in transmission clusters were from patients with prior NICU admission, and
importantly, each of these 7 clusters contained at least one genome collected within the NICU.
In Cluster 1, all 4 non-NICU isolates were from Patient 111, who had been admitted to the NICU despite
having no positive surveillance samples. In Cluster 2, 2 non-NICU isolates were from Patient 257, who
had both positive surveillance and blood culture isolates from the NICU period, and 1 isolate was from
Patient 161 during their NICU admission. The inclusion of these non-NICU isolates in Clusters 1 and 2
did not alter cluster composition or the classification of strains as invasive or colonizing. For smaller
clusters, single or multiple non-NICU isolates were identified: Cluster 10 (1 isolate, Patient 245),
Cluster 29 (1 genome, Patient 534), Cluster 37 (3 genomes, Patient 467), Cluster 51 (2 genomes from
Patient 330 and 1 genome from Patient 331), and Cluster 58 (4 genomes, Patient 36).
Collectively, the hospital-wide sampling including non-NICU isolates provided essential
epidemiological context without compromising the integrity of our NICU-focused transmission analysis.
The predominance of non-overlapping strains outside the NICU supports our hypothesis that most
infants acquired S. aureus through transmission within the NICU rather than from hospital-wide
circulation, while the small subset of NICU-linked isolates detected post-transfer reveals clinically
important patterns of strain persistence that would remain invisible under NICU-restricted sampling. Far
from introducing noise, this comprehensive approach strengthens both the specificity of our
transmission inference and the clinical relevance of our findings.
